DISSERTATION THEOLOGICAL ON THE REMISSION OF SINS g[?]

units.la: C[illegible, ~6 letters] lucratus fuerit mundun beatus & felix haberi cator & inimicus Dei
units.tr: C[illegible, ~6 letters] had gained the world, is to be held blessed and happy, and is a friend of the world and an enemy of God.
Theological Dissertation on the Remission of Sins.
The Reward.

units.la: QUANQUAM honos, virtus, divitiæ, voluptates titillationes corporis apud filios hujus seculi pro cujusquè gustu & vertigine primas tenent, imò homo totum mundum lucraretur, à vera tamen felicitate quantum aberret, Mathæus monstrat Quid enim prodest cuipiam, si totum [illegible, ~8 letters]n, animâ verò suâ mulctetur. Sed is & dici potest, qui quanquàm pec-[illegible, ~6 letters], Deum tamen habet sibi faventem & propitium, (quod omnium religionum primum fundamentum) nam ex Dei inimico amicus & ex peccatore sanctus Dei evadit, & qui Deum habet, omnia habet sibi amica, habet remissionem peccatorum, & qui remissionem peccatorum habet vitam & salutem æternam (inquit Lutherus) & David beatum prædicat, cui non imputat vel remittit Deus peccata, Psal.32. v.2. Quid verè sit illa beatitudo sive felicitas disputatione hacce tractante de Remissione peccatorum videbimus, quam in proflictum damus.
units.tr: Although honour, virtue, riches and bodily pleasures and delights hold the first place among the children of this age, each according to his own taste and giddiness, and although a man should gain the whole world, Matthew shows how far he is from true happiness: For what does it profit anyone if he gains the whole world and loses his soul? But he may also be called happy who, although he is a sinner, nevertheless has God favourable and propitious to him, which is the first foundation of all religions: for from being God's enemy he becomes a friend, and from a sinner a saint of God, and he who has God has all things friendly to him, he has the remission of sins, and he who has the remission of sins has life and eternal salvation (says Luther), and David pronounces blessed the one whose sins God does not impute or remit, Ps. 32:2. What true blessedness or happiness is will be seen in this disquisition, which deals with the remission of sins and which we now put forward for examination.
THESIS I.

units.la: Remissio peccatorum (quæ nihil aliud est, quàm peccata tegere aut non imputare, Psal.32. v.1. 2. Rom. 4. v.7. 8.) est actio Dei gratuita, quâ propter meritum Christi homini gratis imputatum à spiritu sancto applicatum, sola & verâ fide apprehensum fontem & morti æternæ obnoxium, sed verè resipiscentem à peccato & morte absolvit, ad Dei gloriam & hominis salutem.
units.tr: Remission of sins (which is nothing other than covering sins or not imputing them, Ps. 32:1, 2; Rom. 4:7, 8) is a gratuitous act of God, by which, on account of the merit of Christ imputed to man freely, applied by the Holy Spirit and apprehended by true faith alone, he absolves from sin and death a man who is liable to eternal death but who truly repents of sin and death, to the glory of God and the salvation of man.
II.

units.la: Consistit itaquè peccatorum remissio non in radicali peccatorum extirpatione. Rom. 7. v.14. 17. 18. 20. 23. 24. & Gal.5. v.17. 1.Joh.1. v.8. Matth.6. v.12. sed in non imputatione. Psal.32. v.2. Esai.38. v.17. 2.Cor.5. v.19. Ezech.18. v.22. Matth.18. v.27. Pœnarum promeritarum ablatione. Psal.103. v.10. Luc.1. v.77. Rom.8. v.1.
units.tr: The remission of sins consists therefore not in the radical extirpation of sins, Rom. 7:14, 17, 18, 20, 23, 24; Gal. 5:17; 1 John 1:8; Matt. 6:12, but in the non-imputation, Ps. 32:2; Isa. 38:17; 2 Cor. 5:19; Ezek. 18:22; Matt. 18:27, and in the removal of the punishments deserved, Ps. 103:10; Luke 1:77; Rom. 8:1.
III.

units.la: Author tanti beneficii est Jehova, qui solus est judex vitæ & necis, condonans iniquitatem & defectionem & peccatum. Jer.31. v.34. Ego, ego ipse deleo defectiones tuas propter me & peccatorum tuorum non recordor. Esai. 43. v.25. Mich.7. v.18.19. isque solus; Marc.2. v.7. quis potest remittere peccata, nisi solus Deus. Luc.5. v.21. Ratio 1. Deus solus est Νομοθέτης, Jac.4. v.12. In quem proprie peccatur, eatur, Psal. si. v. 6. Solus per peccata lædītur, ergò solus proprie peccata remittere potest. Ratio 2. Solus est καρδιογνώστης[?], 1. Reg. 8. v. 39. Ergò solus peccata remittere potest, & ita conscientias peccatis vexatas tranquillare. Ratio 3. Deus solus Judex est, ergò solus ad condonandum αὐτοξούσιος[?], quia solius Judicis hæc est prærogativa, & reum absolvere & delicta condonare posse. Hinc pii ab eo solo semper remissionem peccatorum petierunt, secundùm Domini præceptum. Matth. 6. v. 12. Luc. 11. v. 4.
units.tr: The author of so great a benefit is Jehovah, who alone is the judge of life and death, pardoning iniquity and transgression and sin, Jer. 31:34: I, I myself blot out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins; Isa. 43:25; Mic. 7:18, 19, and he alone: Mark 2:7: Who can forgive sins but God alone? Luke 5:21. Reason 1: God alone is the lawgiver [νομοθέτης], James 4:12. It is against him properly that sin is committed, Ps. 51:6. He alone is wounded by sins, and therefore he alone can properly remit sins. Reason 2: He alone is the searcher of hearts [καρδιογνώστης], 1 Kings 8:39. Therefore he alone can remit sins and so calm consciences vexed by sins. Reason 3: God alone is judge, and therefore he alone, with authority of his own [αὐτοξούσιος], is able to pardon, because it is the prerogative of the judge alone both to absolve the guilty and to forgive offences. Hence the godly have always sought remission of sins from him alone, according to the Lord's command, Matt. 6:12; Luke 11:4.
IV.

units.la: Rejicimus ergò Pontif. Rom. solutionis peccatorum lepidam potiùs detestandam promissionem, Ps. si. v. 3. 6. Dan. 9. tot. Cap.
units.tr: We therefore reject the Roman Papists' pleasant, rather detestable promise of settling sins, Ps. 51:3, 6; Dan. 9, whole chapter.
V.

units.la: Est actio Dei ὑποδικῶς[?] considerati: pro natura autem operum ad extra convenit omnibus tribus personis SS. Trinitatis; Patri enim etiamsi Judicis partes agit, condonando nobis peccata Matth. 18. v. 35. Filio, qui sponsoris, vadis & Advocati partibus fungitur, merendo (redimeeum, ne descendat in foveam, ego lytrum inveni, Job. 33. v. 24. Justus meus servus justificabit multos cognitione sui, Esai. 53. v. 11.) Unde Paralytico dicebat, confide fili, remissa sunt tibi peccata tua, & comprobat præsenti miraculo, potestatem habere filium hominis in terra remittendi peccata, Matth. 9. v. 2. 6. Marc. 2. v. 5. 10. Luc. 5: 20. 24. & cap. 7. v. 48. 49. remittit 1. Deitate, quia verus Deus. Matth. 9. v. 3. 2. Potestate à patre accepta, Joh. 5. v. 22. & cap. 17. v. 2. 3. Satisfactione, Eph. 1. v. 7. Spiritui sancto, Obsignando, Cancellarii cœlestis quasi partes obit, imò & arrhabonis & obsidis, hoc diploma in cordibus nostris confirmat & obsignat, ingeminans & clamans in cordibus nostris. Gal. 4. v. 6. Eph. 1: 13. 14. Rom. 8. v. 16. In quem non minus peccatur, quàm in Patrem & filium, Act.5.v.3.&4. Eò nos ducit ipse Baptismus, qui confertur in remissionem peccatorum.
units.tr: It is an act of God considered as judge; but according to the nature of his outward works it belongs to all three persons of the Holy Trinity. For the Father, although he acts the part of judge, forgives us our sins, Matt. 18:35. The Son, who fulfils the part of surety, bondsman and advocate, merits it (Deliver him from going down into the pit, I have found a ransom, Job 33:24; By his knowledge my righteous servant shall justify many, Isa. 53:11). Hence he said to the paralytic, Be of good cheer, son, your sins are forgiven you, and by a present miracle he proves that the Son of Man has power on earth to remit sins, Matt. 9:2, 6; Mark 2:5, 10; Luke 5:20, 24; and ch. 7:48, 49. He remits by (1) his deity, because he is true God, Matt. 9:3; (2) the power received from the Father, John 5:22; and ch. 17:2; (3) his satisfaction, Eph. 1:7. The Holy Spirit, by sealing, performs the part of the heavenly registrar, and indeed of the earnest and pledge: he confirms and seals this charter in our hearts, repeating and crying out in our hearts, Gal. 4:6; Eph. 1:13, 14; Rom. 8:16. Against him, no less than against the Father and the Son, sin is committed, Acts 5:3, 4. To this Baptism itself leads us, which is conferred for the remission of sins.
VI.

units.la: Causa [illegible, ~10 letters] non est essentialis Dei justitia, ut Osiander, non ipsa fides actusque credendi per acceptilationem gratuitam ut Arminiani; non Obedientia novæ vitæ ut Sociniani & Anabap; non habitualis & inhærens Justitia in fide & charitate aliisque bonis operibus confistens, quibus promereamur remissionem peccatorum ut Pontif; sed est Dei Misericordia, Gratia & Benignitas, Num.14:19. condona quàsò iniquitatem populi hujus pro magnitudine benignitatis tuæ, Psal.25.v.6.7. & plurimis locis.
units.tr: The cause of justification is not the essential justice of God, as Osiander holds; nor faith itself and the act of believing through a gratuitous acceptilation, as the Arminians hold; nor the obedience of the new life, as the Socinians and Anabaptists hold; nor the habitual and inherent righteousness consisting in faith and charity and other good works, by which we might merit the remission of sins, as the Papists hold. It is rather the mercy, grace and kindness of God, Num. 14:19: Pardon, I beg you, the iniquity of this people according to the greatness of your mercy; Ps. 25:6, 7, and in very many places.
VII.

units.la: Præterea ita fit nostra justificatio ex gratia, ut opera legis & omnis plane gloriatio operum tollatur, Rom.3.v.27. quippe omnis nostra justitia & obedientia, si cum legis ἀνεξιβεία[?] sive cum remissione peccatorum conferatur, imperfectionis arguitur; hinc pii Israelitæ hac confessione utuntur, sumus ut immundus omnes nos, & sicut panniculus abjectissimus omnes nostræ justitiæ, Esai.64:6. & Psal.143:2. Luc.17:10. Etiam in ipso Abrahamo Rom.4:2. Similiter David non operibus, sed remissione peccatorum justificatos, beatos prædicat, Psal.32.v.2. Publicanus gratiam Dei implorans, obtinuit remissionem peccatorum suorum, cùm Pharisæus opera sua jactans & justitiæ suæ confidens, ab eadem fuerit exclusus, Luc.18.v.14. Nullo habito respectu bonorum operum nostrorum, præterquàm enim quòd meritum gratiam excludit, Rom.11:6. Bona opera ante remissionem peccatorum nulla sunt. Eô nos ducit ipsa notatio vocis remissionis, nihil enim aliud designat, quàm peccatorum omnium gratuitam condonationem, Matth.18.v.26.27. (remittere enim & pro peccatis satisfacere sunt contraria. Quicunquè enim sua obtendunt merita & satisfactiones Deo, non ejus misericordiam implorant, sed judicium appellant) non venit Deus (verba Augustini) in Psalm.43. ad inspectionem meritorum, sed ad peccatorum remissionem, non fuisti & factus es, quid Deo dedisti, malus fuisti & liberatus es, quid Deo dedisti, quid non ab eo gratis accepisti? merito & gratia nominatur, quia gratis datur.
units.tr: Moreover, our justification is so from grace that the works of the law and every kind of glorying in works is taken away, Rom. 3:27. For indeed all our righteousness and obedience, if it is compared with the strict demand of the law or with the remission of sins, is shown to be imperfect. Hence the godly Israelites use this confession: We are all become like one unclean, and all our righteousnesses are like a filthy rag, Isa. 64:6; Ps. 143:2; Luke 17:10. This is true even of Abraham himself, Rom. 4:2. Similarly David pronounces blessed those justified not by works but by the remission of sins, Ps. 32:2. The publican, imploring the grace of God, obtained the remission of his sins, whereas the Pharisee, boasting of his works and trusting in his own righteousness, was excluded from the same, Luke 18:14. No regard being had to our good works, for apart from the fact that merit excludes grace, Rom. 11:6, good works are nothing before the remission of sins. The very meaning of the word "remission" leads us to this, for it signifies nothing other than the free pardoning of all sins, Matt. 18:26, 27 (for to remit and to make satisfaction for sins are opposites. For whoever puts forward his own merits and satisfactions to God does not implore his mercy but appeals to his judgment). God does not come (the words of Augustine) to the examination of merits, but to the remission of sins; in Psalm 43. You were not, and you were made; what did you give to God? You were bad and you were set free; what did you give to God? What did you not receive freely from him? It is called merit and grace because it is given freely.
VIII.

units.la: Sed regerunt Pontif. quòd homo propter meritum, Christi gratiâ habituali præditus, si illa suâ gratiâ benè utatur, de condigno augmentum gratiæ hujus mereatur. ℞.
units.tr: But the Papists reply that man, endowed with the habitual grace of Christ, if he makes good use of that grace, merits by condign merit an increase of this grace. Reply:

units.la: 1. Hujus distinctionis fundamentum nullum extat in scriptura. ℞. 2. Hæc distinctio pertinet ad satisfactionem. ℞. 3. Nulla planè dantur merita, quia omnia opera nostra sunt imperfecta, etiam quæ à gratia habituali proveniunt; adhæc illa sunt debita, ut quamvis omnia fecerimus, quæ præcepta sunt, quod tamen nemo sanus jactabit, tamen servi sumus inutiles, nam fecimus tantùm id, quod debuimus, Luc.17.v.10. Nequè tandem nostra sunt, nequè adæquata præmio. Adhæc si per opera non possumus justificari, multò minus mereri. Denique qui per legem vult justificari,debitor est totius legis servandæ, qui autem impegerit in uno tantùm, reus est omnium, at in multis impingimus omnes, adeoque sub maledictione legis sunt, qui per illam justificari prætendunt, tantùm abest, ut quid mereantur.
units.tr: 1. There is no foundation for this distinction anywhere in Scripture. Reply: 2. This distinction pertains to satisfaction. Reply: 3. No merits at all are given, because all our works are imperfect, even those that proceed from habitual grace; moreover they are owed: so that although we have done all the things that are commanded, which no sane person will boast, we are nevertheless unprofitable servants, for we have only done what we ought to have done, Luke 17:10. Nor are they finally our own, nor adequate to the reward. Furthermore, if we cannot be justified by works, much less can we merit anything by them. Finally, whoever wishes to be justified by the law is a debtor to keep the whole law, and whoever stumbles in one point only is guilty of all; but we all stumble in many, and so those who pretend to be justified by the law are under its curse, so far are they from meriting anything.
IX.

units.la: Causa θεοκαταρτικὴ[?] sive meritoria est plenissima Christi satisfactio, quæ consistit in ejus obedientia usquè ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, de qua loquuntur varia sacræ scripturæ loca, Esai.53.4.5. Morbos nostros ipse pertulit & dolores nostros bajulavit, ipse dolore afficitur à defectionibus nostris, atteritur ab iniquitatibus nostris, castigatio pacis nostra imponitur ei, & tumice ejus sit curatio nobis, v. 10. Quandoquè ipse exponebat se sacrificium pro reatu. Mat. 20: 28. cap. 26: 28. Act. 20: 28. 2. Cor. 5: 21. Eph. 1:7. Matth. 1:21. aliis locis.
units.tr: The meritorious cause (the Greek term is uncertain) is the most complete satisfaction of Christ, which consists in his obedience even unto death, indeed the death of the cross, of which various passages of Holy Scripture speak: Isaiah 53:4, 5. He himself bore our diseases and carried our sorrows; he is afflicted by our transgressions, crushed by our iniquities; the chastisement of our peace was laid upon him, and by his stripes we are healed, v. 10. Since he gave himself as a sacrifice for guilt. Matt. 20:28; 26:28; Acts 20:28; 2 Cor. 5:21; Eph. 1:7; Matt. 1:21; and other places.
X.

units.la: Injurii igitur sunt in Christum & ejus satisfactionem, qui alios mediatores & Advocatos huic associant, aliosque satisfactionis modos comminiscuntur. Sic enim 1. Joh. 2: 1. 2. Act. 4: 12.
units.tr: They therefore do wrong to Christ and his satisfaction who associate with him other mediators and advocates, and devise other modes of satisfaction. For thus 1 John 2:1, 2; Acts 4:12.
XI.

units.la: Etiamsi in thesi 6. diximus, nos misericordiâ gratiâ & benignitate remissionem peccatorum consequi, thesi verò 9. per [?]ἀντίλυτρον Filii (remissio verò peccatorum gratuita cum Dei veritate & justitia videtur pugnare, ut Gen. 2. v. 17.) non pugnat nec impingimus, nam hæc duo minimè pugnant, gratiâ & merito nos remissionem peccatorum consequi, Christi enim meritum subordinatur gratiæ & dependet ab ea, quia illa subordinatio est gratia, ut esset propitiatio per meritum suum: adeò ut quâ iram Dei placatam per filium respicimus, habeamus meritum, scilicet Christi pro nobis. Hinc dulcissimæ voces illæ Evang. Joh. 3: 16. Jes. 53: 4. 5. 1. Joh. 1: 7. Rom. 8:3. Col. 2:14. Gratiam tamen etiam, quâ illud nobis gratis donat & imputat.
units.tr: Although in thesis 6 we said that we obtain the remission of sins by God's mercy, grace and kindness, and in thesis 9, through the ransom of the Son (and the free remission of sins seems to clash with God's truth and justice, as in Gen. 2:17), we do not contradict ourselves nor oppose these points. For these two do not conflict: that we obtain the remission of sins by grace and by merit. For Christ's merit is subordinated to grace and depends upon it, since that subordination is itself grace, that there should be propitiation through his merit; so that, insofar as we look to God's wrath appeased through the Son, we have a merit, namely Christ's, on our behalf. Hence those most sweet words of the Gospel: John 3:16; Isa. 53:4, 5; 1 John 1:7; Rom. 8:3; Col. 2:14. Yet we also acknowledge the grace by which he gives and imputes this to us freely.
XII.

units.la: Imputationem hanc meriti Christi melius exprimere non possumus, quàm verbis Catechis. Heidelb. dumconfitemur, quòd sit illa (quâ mihi perfecta satisfactio, justitia & sanctitas Christi imputatur ac donatur, perinde ac si nec ullum peccatum admisissem, nec ulla labes mihi inhæreret, imò quasi eam obedientiam, quam Christus pro me præstitit, ipse perfectè præstitissem.)
units.tr: We cannot express this imputation of Christ's merit better than in the words of the Heidelberg Catechism, when we confess that it is (the way by which the perfect satisfaction, righteousness and holiness of Christ is imputed and given to me, just as if I had never committed any sin, nor any stain had clung to me; indeed, as if I had myself perfectly performed the obedience which Christ performed for me.)
XIII.

units.la: Sed Inst: si cum compensatione, ergò non gra-tis &c. ℞. Respectu Christi Deus gratis non remittit peccata, sed intuitu nostri, satisfactio propriè est Christi, non nostra; Imputatur verò nobis per fidem nullo nostro merito interveniente, Rom.3. v.25. Eph.2:4.5.6.
units.tr: But the objection: if it is with compensation, then it is not free, etc. Answer: With respect to Christ, God does not remit sins freely, but with regard to us; the satisfaction is properly Christ's, not ours; it is imputed to us through faith, with no merit of ours intervening. Rom. 3:25; Eph. 2:4, 5, 6.
XIV.

units.la: Nec Injustus propterea dicendus est Deus, quòd peccata in innocente suo filio puniat, cùm subrogatio Mediatoris in locum hominum debendi reorum, justitiæ Dei non adversetur, quod vel totus cultus Leviticus, in quo peccatoris locum subibat victima, testatur.
units.tr: Nor is God for that reason to be called unjust, because he punishes sins in his innocent Son, since the substitution of the Mediator in place of men, who were the debtors and guilty, does not oppose the justice of God, as the whole Levitical worship testifies, in which the sacrificial victim took the place of the sinner.
XV.

units.la: Rejicimus ergò opiniones Remonstrantium, quâ fidem nobis in locum remissionis peccatorum imputari volunt, quia enim in legis fœdere homo propter carnis impotentiam servari non poterat; volunt, Deum aliud fœdus Evangelicum paululùm mitigatum cum hominibus inivisse, quo obedientia fidei exigatur, & proinde illam fidem, tanquàm partem obedientiæ debitæ, nobis imputari in locum remissionis peccatorum; sed cùm scriptura soli Christi merito perfectam satisfactionem & solutionem tribuat, non potest fides nostra vel obedientia fidei nostra satisfactio vel pars aliqua illius pretii esse; Deinde quòd si fides esset obedientia mandatorum, Apostolus absurdissimam committeret tautologiam, dum dicit, quòd fide justificemur non operibus, Rom.3: 28. adde quòd ipsa fides sit donum Dei & obedientia fructus fidei, 1.Tim.1:s. ergò non meritum pro peccatis.
units.tr: We therefore reject the opinions of the Remonstrants, who wish that faith be imputed to us in place of the remission of sins. For since man, on account of the weakness of the flesh, could not be preserved under the covenant of the law, they hold that God entered into another, somewhat milder, evangelical covenant with men, in which the obedience of faith is required, and therefore that this faith, as a part of the obedience owed, is imputed to us in place of the remission of sins. But since Scripture ascribes perfect satisfaction and payment to the merit of Christ alone, our faith, or the obedience of our faith, cannot be our satisfaction or any part of that price. Furthermore, if faith were the obedience of the commandments, the Apostle would commit a most absurd tautology when he says that we are justified by faith, not by works, Rom. 3:28. Add that faith itself is the gift of God and the obedience is the fruit of faith, 1 Tim. 1:5; therefore it is not a merit for sins.
XVI.

units.la: Pontificii hac in parte paululùm faniores sunt Remonstrantibus, dum satisfactionem Christi veri filii Dei pro peccatis nostris admittant, quamvis illam non parùm extenuent suis satisfactionibus humanis & meritis propriis saltem pro peccatis post baptismum commissis & venialibus; sed non ab actualibus tantùm verùm etiam originali reatu peccati & macula sanguis J. C. F. Dei nos purgat, 1. Joh. 1. v. 7. Rom. 8: 1. 2. Cor. 7: 1. quod purgatorium excludit purgatorium Pontif. omnesquè quaeftuofas indulgentiarum nundinationes, missas, uno verbò merita de congruo & condigno, confectum opus operatum.
units.tr: The Papists are in this respect a little saner than the Remonstrants, in that they admit Christ's satisfaction, the true Son of God, for our sins, although they greatly diminish it by their human satisfactions and their own merits, at least for sins committed after baptism and for venial sins. But it is not only from actual guilt but also from original guilt and stain of sin that the blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, cleanses us: 1 John 1:7; Rom. 8:1, 2; 2 Cor. 7:1. This excludes the Papal purgatory and all the gainful trafficking of indulgences, the masses, in a word, the merits of congruity and condignity, and the work wrought by the work performed.
XVII.

units.la: Et quod dextrâ concesserunt, sinistrâ recipiunt; putant, absurdum esse & ridiculum, nos propter alienam justitiam justificari. Sed 1. ita loquimur cum fcriptura, 2. sepositis aliis rationibus non habent, quod mirentur, cùm ipsi merita Martyrum & satisfactiones humanas velint, posse per indulgentias papales applicari, quod non aliter, quàm imputatione poterit fieri, ut quod unus fuperogatione fecit, alter fecisse id censeatur, adeoquè meritis Christi derogant, quod hominibus adscribere blasphemè non verentur. Saniores tamen sunt Remonstrantes, quòd hi justificationem fidei, id est, observationi legis ex viribus nostris praestitae vendicent, sed Pontificij & Remonstrantes, dum aliud extra Christum salutis meritum, aliam peccatorum expiationem agnoscunt, nihil aliud faciunt, quàm ipsum Christum abnegare.
units.tr: And what they have granted with the right hand, they take back with the left: they think it absurd and ridiculous that we should be justified on account of another's righteousness. But (1) we speak thus with Scripture; (2) setting other arguments aside, they have no reason to wonder, since they themselves want the merits of martyrs and human satisfactions to be applicable through papal indulgences, which cannot be done except by imputation, so that what one has done by supererogation is reckoned as done by another; and thus they detract from the merits of Christ, which they do not hesitate to ascribe blasphemously to men. The Remonstrants are, however, more sound in that they claim justification by faith, that is, by the observance of the law performed from our own powers. But the Papists and the Remonstrants, while they acknowledge another merit of salvation and another expiation of sins apart from Christ, do nothing else than deny Christ himself.
XVIII.

units.la: Subjectum seu Objectum est fons seu peccator. Rom. 3:7.8. & irae filii. Eph. 2:3. sed verè resipiscens seu Christo datus, Joh. 17: 6. & 9. dico fontem sed verè resipiscentem, quod asseritur, quòd ullô pacto non absolvat fontem &c. satis innuitur, non omnibus Deum condonare peccata, sed aliquibus tantùm, iis videlicet, qui resipiscunt & credunt, quod passim in scriptura docetur, Esai. 1: 18. & Matth. 13: 15.
units.tr: The subject, or object, is the fountain or the sinner, Rom. 3:7, 8. and the child of wrath, Eph. 2:3. but one who truly repents or is given to Christ, John 17:6 and 9. When I say "the fountain, but one who truly repents," the claim that he does not in any way absolve the fountain, etc., sufficiently implies that God does not forgive sins to everyone, but only to some, namely those who repent and believe. This is taught throughout Scripture, Isa. 1:18 and Matt. 13:15.
XIX.

units.la: Ratio thes. præced. est evidentissima, cùm enim resipiscentia & fides sint conditiones novi fœderis. Marc. 1: 15. Act. 2: 37. 38. Remissio autem peccatorum præcipuum illius beneficium, Luc. 1: 77. Rom. 11: 27. Heb. 8: 10. 11. 12. Sequitur eam non nisi resipiscentibus & credentibus obtingere. Alias quoque assignatur in scriptura. 1. Agnoscentibus & confitentibus peccata, Prov. 28: 13. 1. Joh. 1: 9. præterita non nocent, (inquit August.) si præsentia non placebunt. 2. Invocantibus Deum, Psal. 86[?]: 5. Dan. 9: 18. Matth. 9: 2. Officium invocationis à cunctis exigit fidelibus, Psal. 32: 6. 3. Diligentibus Deum, Luc. 7: 47. 4. Benè agentibus, Gen. 4: 7. 5. Remittentibus proximo offensas, Mat. 6: 12. 14. 15. Matth. 18. v. ult. Marc. 11: 25. Luc. 6: 37. Quæ omnia in verè resipiscentibus concurrunt.
units.tr: The reason for the preceding thesis is most evident. Since repentance and faith are the conditions of the new covenant, Mark 1:15; Acts 2:37, 38, and the forgiveness of sins is its chief benefit, Luke 1:77; Rom. 11:27; Heb. 8:10–12, it follows that this benefit comes only to those who repent and believe. Scripture also assigns other conditions: (1) forgiveness is given to those who acknowledge and confess their sins, Prov. 28:13; 1 John 1:9. "Past sins do no harm," says Augustine, "if present sins do not please." (2) It is given to those who call upon God, Ps. 86:5; Dan. 9:18; Matt. 9:2. The duty of calling upon God is required of all the faithful, Ps. 32:6. (3) It is given to those who love God, Luke 7:47. (4) It is given to those who do well, Gen. 4:7. (5) It is given to those who forgive their neighbours' offences, Matt. 6:12, 14, 15; Matt. 18, last verse; Mark 11:25; Luke 6:37. All of these concur in those who truly repent.
XX.

units.la: Excluduntur igitur. 1. Homines non resipiscentes, quos idcircò ne unquam novisse dicet in ultimo die, Matth. 7: 23.
units.tr: Excluded, therefore, are: (1) those who do not repent, whom at the last day he will say he never knew, Matt. 7:23.
XXI.

units.la: Angeli tùm mali, quibus Deus omnem reconciliationis spem præcidit, Jud. v. 6. 2. Pet. 2: 4. tùm boni, qui cùm Deum per peccatum non offenderint, reconciliatione per mediatorem non habent opus.
units.tr: The angels: the evil ones, for whom God has cut off all hope of reconciliation, Jude 6; 2 Pet. 2:4; and the good ones, who, since they have not offended God by sin, have no need of reconciliation through a mediator.
XXII.

units.la: Omnis igitur V. & N. T. remissionis peccatorum fons & causa est Christus, neque enim alia vitæ æternæ consequendæ ratio in V. quàm in N. T. non est quò eas, nisi ad Christum, non est quà eas, nisi per Christum, Joh. 14: 6. Act. 4: 12. & 15: 11. Heb. 13: 8.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the fountain and cause of the forgiveness of sins in the whole of the Old and New Testaments. For there is no other way of obtaining eternal life in the Old Testament than in the New. There is no "whither" to go except to Christ, and no "way" to go except through Christ, John 14:6; Acts 4:12; 15:11; Heb. 13:8.
XXIII.

units.la: Beneficium ipsum, quod spectat, est condonatio peccatorum, imò omnis generis, minimorum, & maximorum, omnium.
units.tr: The benefit itself which is in view is the pardon of sins, indeed of every kind, of the smallest and of the greatest, of all.
XXIV.

units.la: Deus condonat peccata, Psal. 32: 1. Esai. 38: 17. & cap. 43: 12. cap. 44: 17. Jer. 31: 34. Omnis generis, non tantùm minima, sed etiam maxima imò omnia. Condonans iniquitatem & defectionem & peccatum, Exod. 34: 7. Jer. 33: 8. Et mundabo eos ab omni iniquitate ipsorum, qua peccaverint mihi & condonabo omnes iniquitates ipsorum, quibus peccaverint mihi, & quibus deficientes rebellaverint, Ezech. 36: 25. Act. 13: 38. 39. Col. 2: 13. 1. Joh. 1: 7. Esai. 38: 17. Reatum & pœnam, Psal. 32: 2. Mich. 7: v. 19. Rom. 3: 24. Eph. 1. v. 7. Servi cœlestis exemplo, Matth. 18: 25. Confirmatur quoquè rationibus. 1. A sufficientia J. C. utpotè quæ est adæquata justitiæ divinæ, quod patet tùm ex dignitate personæ satisfacientis, quæ est ipse Deus, Act. 20: 28. Dominus gloriæ, 1. Cor. 2: 8. Filius Dei, 1. Joh. 1: 7. Filius unigeniti, Joh. 3: 16. Proprius, Rom. 8: 32. tùm ex gravitate pœnæ, quæ passionem, crucifixionem, mortem, sepulturam & descensum ad inferos complectitur. 2. A Misericordia Dei plane infinita, cui omnia peccata nostra, quantacunquè sint, non magis resistere possunt, quàm scintilla in mare cadens stare potest.
units.tr: God pardons sins, Ps. 32:1; Isa. 38:17; 43:12; 44:17; Jer. 31:34. Of every kind: not only the smallest, but also the greatest, indeed all. He pardons iniquity and transgression and sin, Exod. 34:7; Jer. 33:8: "And I will cleanse them from all their iniquity by which they have sinned against me, and I will pardon all their iniquities by which they have sinned against me and by which they have rebelled through their defections," Ezek. 36:25; Acts 13:38, 39; Col. 2:13; 1 John 1:7; Isa. 38:17. He pardons guilt and punishment, Ps. 32:2; Mic. 7:19; Rom. 3:24; Eph. 1:7. The example of the heavenly servant, Matt. 18:25. It is also confirmed by reasons. (1) From the sufficiency of Jesus Christ, which is adequate to divine justice. This is clear both from the dignity of the person who satisfies, who is God himself, Acts 20:28; the Lord of glory, 1 Cor. 2:8; the Son of God, 1 John 1:7; the Son of the only-begotten, John 3:16; his own Son, Rom. 8:32; and from the weight of the punishment, which comprises the passion, crucifixion, death, burial and descent into hell. (2) From the God of mercy, who is wholly infinite, to whom none of our sins, however great they may be, can offer more resistance than a spark falling into the sea can withstand.
XXV.

units.la: Ad primam rationem quæritur, si sufficientia Christi est adæquata justitiæ divinæ & satisfactum, quare non remittuntur quoque peccata reproborum, quod videtur probari ex prima ratione præced. thes. ℛ. Deum nec plus nec minus exegisse, quàm quod justitia postulabat; deindè sic placuit.
units.tr: To the first reason the question is raised: if the sufficiency of Christ is adequate to divine justice and satisfaction has been made, why are the sins of the reprobate not also remitted? This seems to follow from the first reason of the preceding thesis. Answer: God did not require more nor less than justice demanded; and then, it pleased him so.
XXVI.

units.la: Ad alteram rationem movetur quæstio, si misericordia Dei planè est infinita, nec omnis generis peccata magis resistere possunt quàm scintilla in mare cadens, quare non quoque remittitur peccatum in spiritum sanctum. ℛ. 1. Pro peccato hoc [illegible, ~10 letters] θυσία, Heb. 10:26. Perindè uti sub lege pro certis quibusdam peccatis nullum Sacrificium expiatorium fuit ordinatum. 2. Insanabile est, nec fieri potest, ut, qui illud patravit ad remissionem unquam perveniat, quia nunquam resipiscentiam est acturus, & gratiam Christi, quo solo unicoque pharmaco peccata nostra tolli, sanariqué possunt, contemptim & summâ petulantia rejicit atqué dedignatur. 3. Deo omninò decretum est illud in justitia sua punire, undè nec divinæ potentiæ aut Misericordiæ vel etiam meritorum Christi defectui, sed solius Dei voluntati & consilio causa hæc est adscribenda. 4. Huic peccato speciatim competit, quòd sit irremissibile, Matth. 12:31.32. Marc. 3:29. Ubi observandum Matthæum per Marcum explicari, nam quod ille dixerat, non iri remissum hoc peccatum, nec in hoc sæculo nec in futuro, hic dicit, quòd quicunquè illo obstringitur, non habet remissionem peccatorum in æternum, sed tenetur æternô judicio, nihil aliud sibi voluit Christus (juxta Chrysostomum,) quàm insinuare, hoc crimen graviter puniendum & in hac vita & in futura.
units.tr: To the second reason the question is raised: if the mercy of God is wholly infinite, and no kind of sin can resist it more than a spark falling into the sea, why is the sin against the Holy Spirit not also forgiven? Answer: (1) For this sin there is [illegible, about ten letters] sacrifice [θυσία], Heb. 10:26, just as under the law no expiatory sacrifice was ordained for certain sins. (2) It is incurable, and it cannot happen that the one who has committed it should ever attain forgiveness, because he will never repent, and he scornfully and with the greatest insolence rejects and disdains the grace of Christ, the only remedy by which our sins can be removed and healed. (3) God has wholly decreed to punish this sin in his justice; hence the cause is not to be ascribed to any defect in the divine power or mercy, or even in the merits of Christ, but solely to the will and counsel of God. (4) It is specifically true of this sin that it is unforgivable, Matt. 12:31, 32; Mark 3:29. Here it must be observed that Matthew is explained by Mark. For what the former said, that this sin will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come, the latter says: whoever is bound by it does not have forgiveness of sins for ever, but is held liable to eternal judgment. According to Chrysostom, Christ meant nothing else than to indicate that this crime is to be punished severely both in this life and in the life to come.
XXVII.

units.la: Instrumentum quod est Evangelium V.& N.T.(nam est potentia Dei ad salutem cuivis credenti, Rom. 1: 16.) obsignatur usu sacramentorum, Circumcisionis, esse signum & sigillum justitiæ fidei, Rom. 4: 11. Baptismi, Marc. 1: 4. Luc. 3: 3. Act. 2: 38.
units.tr: The instrument, which is the Gospel of the Old and New Testament (for it is "the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes," Rom. 1:16), is sealed by the use of the sacraments: of circumcision, which is "a sign and seal of the righteousness of faith," Rom. 4:11; and of baptism, Mark 1:4, Luke 3:3, Acts 2:38.
XXVIII.

units.la: Undè jus peccata remittendi ministerialiter nempè & annunciativè competit legitimis Ecclesiæ ministris, Joh. 20: 23. Si quorum remiseritis peccata, non verò judicialiter & αὐτονομοθετικῶς ut Pontif. qui suis sacrificulis & presbyteris auricularibus absolutè judiciariam peccata remittendi potestatem concedunt.
units.tr: Hence the right to remit sins belongs ministerially, that is, declaratively, to the lawful ministers of the Church, John 20:23, "If you remit the sins of any." It does not belong judicially and autonomothetically, as the Papists hold, who grant to their priests and auricular presbyters an absolute judicial power of remitting sins.
XXIX.

units.la: Instrumentum, quò beneficium hoc accipimus, est fides, non temporaria & miraculorum, sed vera & Christo nitens, hinc fide, ex fide & per fidem nunquàm tamen propter fidem nos remissionem peccatorum consequi & justificari, Rom. 3: 28. Gal. 2: 16. dicitur.
units.tr: The instrument by which we receive this benefit is faith: not a temporary faith of miracles, but a true faith resting on Christ. Hence it is said that by faith, from faith and through faith we obtain remission of sins and are justified, yet never on account of faith, Rom. 3:28, Gal. 2:16.
XXX.

units.la: Sed observa, nam Sociniani hæretici idem præstant; dum enim cum scriptura dicimus, nos per fidem habere remissionem peccatorum, quoquè dicunt, nos per fidem in Christum consequi remissionem peccatorum, ut in ipsorum scriptis legere est; quis hic prima fronte non putaret, hæc esse plane orthodoxa, sed si penitius inspiciemus, quid per fidem in Christum intelligant, apparebit statim virus: Christum enim non sumunt, ut nobis proponitur cum suis meritis verâ fide apprehendendus, sed tantùm ita, ut ei viam salutis annuncianti & vitam æternam sub conditione fidei, id est, obedientiæ suis præceptis præstandæ nobis promittenti confidamus, id enim fidei nomine in Christum ab ipsis intelligitur, quod in rei veritate plane contrarium.
units.tr: But observe this, for the Socinian heretics assert the same thing. When we say with Scripture that we have remission of sins through faith, they also say that we obtain remission of sins through faith in Christ, as may be read in their writings. At first sight anyone would think these were plainly orthodox statements. But if we look more closely at what they mean by faith in Christ, the poison appears at once. For they do not take Christ, as he is set before us, to be apprehended with his merits by true faith; they only trust that he, announcing to us the way of salvation and promising eternal life under the condition of faith, that is, of obedience to his precepts to be rendered by us, is so. For by the name of faith in Christ they understand this, which in the reality of the matter is plainly the opposite.
XXXI

units.la: ℞. 1. Fides & Obedientia se habent instar causæ & effectus, arboris & fructus, 1.Tim.1:5. finis mandati est charitas ex mundo corde, cor autem fide purgatur, ⌣Act. 15.v.9. Causa autem non est ipsum effectum, nec essectum ipsa causa, ergo etiam fides non est ipsa obedientia, sed ipsius causa, nec obedientia est ipsa fides sed ejus efsectum, an vera & viva sit nec ne, ut arbor dignoscitur ex suis fructibus, bona arbor enim profert bonos fructus, Matth.7:17.
units.tr: Ans. 1. Faith and obedience stand to each other as cause and effect, as tree and fruit: 1 Tim. 1:5, The end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of faith unfeigned; Acts 15:9, purifying their hearts by faith. But a cause is not the effect itself, nor is the effect the cause. So faith is not obedience itself but its cause, and obedience is not faith itself but its effect. Whether faith is true and living is known from its obedience, as a tree is known by its fruits: Matt. 7:17, A good tree bringeth forth good fruit.

units.la: ℞. 2. Fidei tribuuntur effecta, quæ nunquam tribuuntur obedientiæ aut operibus. At si fides esset obedientia, parva cum fide haberet effecta, justificatio tantùm tribuitur fidei, Rom.4:3. Joh.1:12.
units.tr: Ans. 2. Effects are ascribed to faith which are never ascribed to obedience or to works. But if faith were obedience, it would have the effects of obedience. Justification is ascribed only to faith: Rom. 4:3; John 1:12.

units.la: ℞. 3. Distinguuntur suis objectis; objectum fidei sunt promissiones Evangelicæ: Objectum verò obedientiæ est lex: Evangelium est norma credendorum, Lex verò faciendorum.
units.tr: Ans. 3. They are distinguished by their objects. The object of faith is the evangelical promises; the object of obedience is the law. The Gospel is the rule of what is to be believed, and the Law the rule of what is to be done.

units.la: ℞. 4. Fides & Obedientia, quæ nihil aliud est, quàm opus, sibi mutuo è diametro opponuntur, ergò non sunt idem, secus nulla esset oppositio; deindè si fides sit obedientia mandatorum, Apostolus absurdissimam comitteret tautologiam. Justificationem fidei tribuendo, & operibus adimendo, dum dicit, fide justificari hominem absque operibus legis, Rom.3:28.
units.tr: Ans. 4. Faith and obedience, which is nothing other than a work, are set diametrically against each other. Therefore they are not the same, for otherwise there would be no opposition. Further, if faith were the obedience of the commandments, the Apostle would commit a most absurd tautology when, in ascribing justification to faith and taking it away from works, he says that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law: Rom. 3:28.

units.la: ℞. 5. Tandem etiam differunt definitionibus; nam fides definitur ab Apostolo, Heb.11:v.1. quòd sit fiducialis apprehensio meriti Christi, Obedientia mandatorum, etiam ex mente adversariorum est impletio legis, differunt ergò genere & forma,
units.tr: Ans. 5. Finally, they also differ in their definitions. The Apostle defines faith, Heb. 11:1, as the confident apprehension of the merit of Christ. Obedience to the commandments, even by the opinion of our adversaries, is the fulfilling of the law. They therefore differ in genus and in form.
XXXII.

units.la: At pestilentissimi hæretici nondum acquiescunt, sed, ut hæc sua mandatorum obedientia in justificationem cederet, non quidem intuitu operum, quasi ea id merentur, dicunt, summâ Dei clementiâ atque misericordiâ fieri, ut nos quamvis non perfectè justi simus, tamen pro talibus reputemur, & ita nobiscum agitur ac si perfectè justi fuissemus.
units.tr: But the most pestilent heretics do not yet give in. So that this their obedience to the commandments may count toward justification, they say that it comes about, not indeed in view of works, as if they merited it, but by the highest clemency and mercy of God, that although we are not perfectly just, we are nevertheless reckoned as such, and so we are dealt with as if we had been perfectly just.
XXXIII.

units.la: Hæc ex parte benè dicta essent, si concederent, illam divinam clementiam inniti satisfactioni Christi pro peccatis nostris loco nostro præstitæ, at quamdiu hoc fundamentum non habent, nihil sani hac de re possunt docere, sed error errorem generabit exitialem; deinde errant in eo, quòd illam observationem mandatorum pro virili sua parte legi præstitam divinâ benignitate ipsis in justitiam putent imputari. Nam 1. illa observatio mandatorum est opus, at justificatio nostri coram Deo constanter operibus adimitur, & quamvis secundum ipsos opus sit imperfe-ctum, nec tamen gratia cum illo potest consistere, quia fides & gratia operibus, non opera imperfecta perfectis opponuntur. 2. Si justificatio fieret ex illa prætensa obedientia, imputatio fieret aliquo modo ex debito, non absolutè ex gratia. 3. Repugnat opus tale imperfe-ctum ex Dei gratia pro persecto haberi, per quandam acceptilationem seu imaginariam solutionem, quæ apud Deum justissimum Judicem locum non habet, cujus judicium est secundùmveritatem, à quo proindè multum abest, ut imperfectum pro perfecto reputet, sed remissio peccatorum
units.tr: These things might be well said in part if they conceded that this divine clemency rests on the satisfaction of Christ rendered in our place for our sins. But as long as they do not have this foundation, they can teach nothing sound on this matter, and error will generate deadly error. Further, they err in this, that they think that the observance of the commandments, which is rendered to the law by each man to the extent of his own ability, is imputed to them for righteousness by the divine kindness. For, first, that observance of the commandments is a work, whereas our justification before God is constantly taken away from works; and although, according to them, the work is imperfect, yet it cannot be consistent with grace, because faith and grace are set against works, not imperfect works against perfect ones. Second, if justification came from that alleged obedience, imputation would take place in some way as a debt, not absolutely from grace. Third, such an imperfect work cannot be held by the grace of God to be perfect, through a certain acceptilation or imaginary payment, which has no place before God, the most just Judge, whose judgment is according to truth. Far from it, then, that he should count the imperfect as perfect; rather, the remission of our sins,

units.la: nostrorum seu nostri justificatio coram Deo tribuitur Christo & ejus satisfactioni pro nobis, sic enim sanguini ejus tribuitur, Eph.1:7. 1.Joh.1:7. & 2:2. Ejus morti & resurrectioni, Rom. 4:25. & ex hoc fonte prodit, quòd obedientia nostra aliàs imperfecta, quæ ex fide procedit, & à nobis spiritu Dei regenerantis præstatur, à Deo tanquàm bonum opus acceptetur, eò quòd illius impersectiones & scoriæ admixtæ obedientiâ Christi perfectâ tegantur, & ita denominatio fiat à meliori parte.
units.tr: or our justification before God, is ascribed to Christ and to his satisfaction for us. So it is ascribed to his blood: Eph. 1:7; 1 John 1:7; 2:2. To his death and resurrection: Rom. 4:25. And from this source it comes about that our obedience, otherwise imperfect, which proceeds from faith and is rendered by us through the Spirit of regenerating God, is accepted by God as a good work, because its imperfections and dross mixed with it are covered by the perfect obedience of Christ, and so the denomination is taken from the better part.
XXXIV.

units.la: Finis ultimus remissionis peccatorum est illustratio gloriæ Dei, gratiæ & misericordiæ, Eph.1:6. Tit.2:11.12. 13. 1.Cor.1:31. 2.Cor.5:19.21.
units.tr: The ultimate end of the remission of sins is the illustration of the glory of God, of his grace and mercy: Eph. 1:6; Titus 2:11, 12, 13; 1 Cor. 1:31; 2 Cor. 5:19, 21.
XXXV.

units.la: Finis proximus est hominis bonum seu salus, ex efsectis intelligitur, Joh.5:24. 1. Adoptio in filios Dei, nam ut nulla est condemnatio iis, qui sunt in Jesu Christo, qui non secundùm carnem, sed secundùm spiritum ambulant, ita quotquot spiritu Dei aguntur, ii sunt filii Dei, adeoquè etiam hæredes, hæredes quidem Dei, cohæredes verò Christi, Rom.8:1.17. quem quotquot exceperunt, dedit eis hoc jus, ut filii Dei sint facti, nempe ijs, qui credunt in nomen ejus, Joh.1:12. 2. Libertas christiana, Joh.8:36. Galat.5:1. 3. Pax conscientiæ, Rom.5:1.2. 4. Liber aditus ad Deum, Heb.4:16. Eph.3:12. 5. Tolerantia crucis, Rom.5:3. 6. Sanctificatio & studium bonorum operum, Tit.2:11.12. 7. Glorificatio & salus æterna.
units.tr: The proximate end is the good or salvation of man, which is understood from its effects: John 5:24. (1) Adoption as sons of God. For as there is no condemnation for those who are in Jesus Christ, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit, so all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God, and therefore also heirs, heirs indeed of God and joint-heirs with Christ: Rom. 8:1, 17. To as many as received him he gave this right, that they should become sons of God, namely to those who believe in his name: John 1:12. (2) Christian liberty: John 8:36; Gal. 5:1. (3) Peace of conscience: Rom. 5:1, 2. (4) Free access to God: Heb. 4:16; Eph. 3:12. (5) Endurance of the cross: Rom. 5:3. (6) Sanctification and zeal for good works: Titus 2:11, 12. (7) Glorification and eternal salvation.
XXXVI.

units.la: Proprietates materiæ nostræ sunt. 1. Remissio peccatorum fit unico actu & semel, Heb.10:2. 2. Est immutabilis juxta naturam Dei, cui repugnat peccata semel remissa iterum punire, ideo Paulo persuasum erat, neque mortem, neque vitam neque Ang: &c. Rom.8: 37.38.39. 3. Est perfecta, expers quoad se omnis in- & decrementi, Jes.43:5. Psalm.103:12. Non per ludum& jocum, sed serio nobiscum agit Deus, remittens, id est non reputans, sed tegens peccata nostra, Psalm.32:1. Liturâm[?] enim gratiose chirographo nostro inducit, lacerat & abjicit. 4. Etiam est certissima, si enim agnoscit bos possessorem suum & asinus praesepe Domini sui, Esai.1:3. quomodo genus electum, regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus quem sibi Deus ut proprium vendicat, virtutes illius non praedicabit, qui vocavit e tenebris in admirabilem suam lucem, 1.Petr. 2:9. Purificat Deus sibi ipsi populum peculiarem, sectatorem bonorum operum, Tit.2:14. Qui per opera purificationis suae & electionis conscius: habens spem hanc in eo sitam, castum se conservat, sicut & ille castus est, 1.Joh.3:23. Rom.5:1. Eph.3:12. 1.Joh.3:14. Jac. 1:6. Interna sp. s. testificatione, Rom.8:15. 1.Cor.2:12. 2.Cor.1:21. Gal.4:6. & aliis locis, inductione exemplorum. Abrah: Rom.4:11.16.18. Job.19:25. Pauli, Rom.8:38.
units.tr: These are the properties of our subject. (1) The remission of sins takes place by a single act and once for all, Heb.10:2. (2) It is unchangeable, in keeping with the nature of God, to whom it is contrary to punish again sins once forgiven. Hence Paul was persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, etc., Rom.8: 37.38.39. (3) It is perfect and, in itself, free from all increase and decrease, Isa.43:5. Ps.103:12. God deals with us not in sport and jest but in earnest, forgiving, that is, not counting our sins but covering them, Ps.32:1. For by grace he brings an erasure to our bond, tears it up and casts it away. (4) It is also most certain. If the ox knows its owner and the ass its master's crib, Isa.1:3. how could God not proclaim the virtues of the chosen race, the royal priesthood, the holy nation, the people whom God claims as his own, of him who called them out of darkness into his marvellous light, 1 Pet. 2:9. God purifies for himself a peculiar people, zealous for good works, Tit.2:14. He who, conscious of his purification and election through works, and having this hope set in him, keeps himself chaste, as he also is chaste, 1 John 3:23. Rom.5:1. Eph.3:12. 1 John 3:14. Jas. 1:6. It is attested by the inward testimony of the Holy Spirit, Rom.8:15. 1 Cor.2:12. 2 Cor.1:21. Gal.4:6. and in other places, by the adduction of examples: Abraham, Rom.4:11.16.18. Job, Job 19:25. Paul, Rom.8:38.
XXXVII.

units.la: Coronodis loco apponam Satanae objectionem, aggravando & ob oculos ponendo nobis nostra innumerabilia peccata, sed Resp. credere, id est, firmiter statuere, remissa esse nobis per Christum omnia peccata; quae consolatio est solius Ecclesiae; Num. 23: 25.26. Jes. 33: 24. Extra eam nulla salus, Joël.2:32. Act.2:47. Eaque princeps & fundamentum omnium reliquarum consolationum. Ubi enim remissio peccatorum est, ibi vita & æterna salus; inquit Lutherus rectè; nam si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos, Rom. 8:31. Exinde existit gloriatio & exultatio illa Apost: Rom. 8: 33. &c. Moveat itaquè hic uberrimus fructus omnes Christianos, hac ex doctrina dimanans. Quis ille? Bona conscientia & deinceps vita perennis. Persuasus enim de remissis peccatis suis omnibus, bonam habet conscientiam. Bona enim conscientia non in eo consistit, ut vulgò putatur, quod quis nullius peccati aut facinoris sibi conscius sit, quis enim verè integer scelerisquè purus, sed in eo, quòd sit certò persuasus, se propitium habere Deum peccatis suis propter Christum remissis. Psalm. 32: 1. Hæc est illa consolatio, hic est ille thesaurus, quem quilibet sibi comparabit, qui rectè sapit, AMEN.
units.tr: By way of a corollary I will add Satan's objection, which aggravates our countless sins and sets them before our eyes. The answer is: to believe, that is, to hold firmly, that all our sins are forgiven us through Christ. This consolation belongs to the Church alone, Num. 23: 25.26. Isa. 33: 24. Outside her there is no salvation, Joel 2:32. Acts 2:47. This consolation is the chief one and the foundation of all the rest. As Luther rightly says: Where there is forgiveness of sins, there is life and eternal salvation. For if God is for us, who is against us, Rom. 8:31. From this arises that boasting and exultation of the Apostle, Rom. 8:33, etc. So this most abundant fruit, flowing from this doctrine, ought to move all Christians. What is it? A good conscience and, thereafter, everlasting life. For one who is persuaded that all his sins have been forgiven has a good conscience. A good conscience does not consist, as is commonly thought, in a man being aware of no sin or crime, for who is truly blameless and pure of wickedness? It consists in being firmly persuaded that God is propitious to him, his sins having been forgiven for Christ's sake, Ps. 32: 1. This is that consolation, this is that treasure, which anyone who is wise will procure for himself. AMEN.
To the Friend and Author, Most Learned in Defence of the Faith.
I.

units.la: Dissimilis nos vena tenet,nec Carbasa ventus Pellit idem, vario labuntur tempora cursu, Cura animos diversa tenet, hic bella Mavortis, Heroumquè animos, & fortia pectora bello Coelo æquat, laetosquè jubet sperare triumphos. Ille peregrinos mores, & dissona Jura Carpit limitibus nunquam digressus avitis. Nec quicquam, nisi quod puerili blacterat ore Miratur. Patriâ tantum mensdiscit in umbra. Hic velut antiquus tutator veteris aurei Mercibus immoritur, studioquè senescit habendi. Incubat ille foris, coecumq; in pectore vulnus Suspirat: nunc laetus aquas, nunc tristis in auras Mentem oculosquè levat, nunc priscum ejurat amorem Transfuga, nunc Dominæ timet amisisse favorem Sed te sancta tenet flammâ meliore Camoena Mysta elues, tacitò verbi correptus amore;
units.tr: Different tides hold us, and the wind does not drive the same sails. Times slip by in varied course. Different cares occupy minds: one man sets the wars of Mars, the hearts of heroes, and brave breasts in battle on a level with heaven, and bids them hope for joyful triumphs. Another carps at foreign manners and foreign laws, never having left his ancestral boundaries. He admires nothing except what he babbles with a childish mouth; he learns only in the shade of his homeland. Here one, like an old guardian of an ancient treasure, dies among his wares and grows old in the eager pursuit of having. That one lies outside, sighing over a hidden wound in his breast; now he lifts his mind and eyes, glad, to the waters, now, sad, to the air; now as a deserter he renounces his former love, now he fears he has lost his lady's favour. But you, Mystes, are held by the holy Muse with a better flame, rapt by the silent love of the Word.

units.la: Tu mentem geniumq; tuum majoribus aufis Erigis, & viridi vestitum tempora daphne Te cupis Aoniis quondam inclarescere chartis En Christus, non Papa-Goel, non Papa sed Abba Ter sonteis salvans diram compescit Erynnin: Et Christi meritum & rubentem sanguinis undam Miramur, sacris fideiq; amplectimur ulnis.
units.tr: You lift up your mind and genius, with greater gifts taken away, and you wish your temples, clothed in green laurel, to become famous one day in Aonian pages. Behold Christ, not a Papa-Goel, not a Pope, but Abba. Saving thrice over, he restrains the dire Erinys. And we marvel at the merit of Christ and the reddened wave of his blood, and embrace them in the holy arms of faith.

units.la: GElyck de roode Zee geheel gedaen verdrincken Het Phaaronsche Heyr, t'vvelck moedig dede blincken Alldus de roode Zee den grooten Ocean K'segge Christus Bloed Versoening vvercken kan Wel Wel Christ Mensche-God sall richten myne Sacken Ende vaster mynen Soen by synen Vader macken Als Jonathan vvel eer vor David heft gedaan Doe tegens hem de Saul met vvrake ging belaën; Vast sondig is myn Sond, edoch heb ick vernomen Van mynen soeten Franck, dat Christus is gekomen Zuyt scheldend my daer van, ten Vader gaet hy in Als mynen Advocat, en mynen Benjamin.
units.tr: Whoever drowned in the Red Sea the Pharaoh's host, which shone so boldly, the same Red Sea can, so to speak, make the great ocean, Christ's blood, work reconciliation. Well, well, Christ, God-man, shall judge my cause and make my Son stand firmer with his Father, as Jonathan once long ago did for David when Saul went out against him in vengeance. My sin is truly sinful, yet I have heard from my sweet friend that Christ has come. Let them scold me for it; he goes in to the Father as my Advocate and my Benjamin.

units.la: Sic utroq; Idiomate gratulabundus ascinit D. G.
units.tr: Thus, rejoicing, he sings in both languages. D. G.
II.

units.la: UNde tibi quæso, dicas, hîc suppetit ardor? Quo vel ad arma omnes nunc pacis tempore poscis: Quid te commoveat, video; nec spes, puto, fallit: Gloria nonne Dei tibi dat certaminis ansam? Ad gratos igitur lætus contende triumphos, Nec dubites, cedat quin mox victoria vobis, Cùm tibi sit clypeus summus moderator Olympi.
units.tr: Whence, I ask you, does this ardour come to you here, that you now call everyone to arms even in a time of peace? What moves you, I see; and I think hope does not deceive. Does not the glory of God give you the occasion for the contest? Therefore hasten joyfully to the welcome triumphs, and do not doubt that victory will soon fall to you, since the highest governor of Olympus is your shield.

units.la: Hæc paucula in honoris & amicitiæ in-æternum duraturæ τεκμήριον accine-re voluit
units.tr: He wished to sing these few lines as a token [τεκμήριον] of honour and of a friendship that will last for ever.
V. H. S. S. M. Cand.
THE END
